Tuberculosis · slides 3–9

Granuloma and tuberculosis basics

Case on the opening slide TB 3

A 30-year-old man with 2 months of cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss; X-ray shows scattered rounded foci, necrosis and a small cavity. Keep him in mind: every part of this lecture explains a piece of his picture.

  • Granuloma TB 4: a chronic specific inflammation. An organised collection of macrophages and other inflammatory cells around a pathogen, in a circular form. It forms when the immune system tries to wall off a pathogen it cannot eliminate. It causes necrosis and replacement of tissue by fibrosis.
  • Tuberculosis TB 5: a chronic infective granuloma caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (tubercle bacilli). Infection by inhalation (coughing or sneezing of an active patient) or ingestion of contaminated milk.

Host–bacteria interaction TB 6

  1. M. tuberculosis reproduces inside macrophages.
  2. Macrophages are unable to present the antigen to lymphocytes.
  3. Bacteria can become dormant → latent infection.
  4. If macrophages do present the antigen → the immune response is activated, with cytokines and tissue necrosis.

Risk groups TB 7

AIDS, overcrowding, malnutrition, close contact with active patients, smoking, alcohol.

Symptoms TB 7

Chronic cough (haemoptysis), fever, night sweats, weight loss. The weight loss gave TB its old name, "consumption".

Mechanisms of caseation TB 9

  1. Hypersensitivity: between lymphokines from T lymphocytes and macrophages and the bacillary antigen (tuberculoprotein).
  2. Ischaemic necrosis: due to endarteritis obliterans.
Granuloma = a wall around a guest that won't leaveMacrophages ring the pathogen they can't kill; the result is necrosis, then fibrosis.
TB risk "A-MOCSA"AIDS, Malnutrition, Overcrowding, Close contact, Smoking, Alcohol.
Caseation has two causes: "Hyper and Hungry"Hypersensitivity (lymphokines vs tuberculoprotein) and ischaemia (endarteritis obliterans starving the centre).
Granuloma is chronic specific inflammation, not acute. TB spreads by inhalation or milk. In the macrophage the bacilli multiply rather than die.

Tuberculosis · slides 10–18

The tubercle, immunity and hypersensitivity

  • Tubercle (tuberculous granuloma) TB 11: the basic unit of tuberculosis. A microscopic collection of chronic inflammatory cells, caseation necrosis and fibrosis around the bacilli: the tissue's reaction to TB.
  • Microscopy slides TB 12–14: caseating tubercle, Langhans giant cell (nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery), TB bacilli inside a giant cell, epithelioid granuloma, caseating TB lymph node.
  • Miliary tuberculosis TB 15–16: a large number of bacilli travel through the blood and spread all over the body, giving many tiny millet-seed tubercles.
ImmunityHypersensitivity
TypeCell-mediatedLymphokine-driven
CellsMacrophages, epithelioid cells, giant cellsSensitised T lymphocytes and macrophages
ResultEngulf bacilli, stop spread → tubercle formationCaseation necrosis

Slide 18. The formative exam on slide 17 asks you to identify a tubercle under the microscope and list its cells: epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes and fibroblasts around central caseation.

Immunity Builds, Hypersensitivity BurnsImmunity builds the tubercle wall; hypersensitivity burns the centre into cheese (caseation).
Read a tubercle from the inside out: "Cheese, Epithelioid, Giant, Lymph, Fibrous"Central caseation, epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, a rim of lymphocytes, fibrosis on the outside.
The tubercle is microscopic. Miliary TB spreads by the blood, not lymph. Caseation comes from hypersensitivity, not from immunity.

Tuberculosis · slides 19–22

Primary and secondary pulmonary tuberculosis

Primary pulmonary TBSecondary pulmonary TB
WhoFirst infection (childhood type)Second infection or reactivation; adult type
LesionPrimary complex: Ghon's focus + tuberculous lymphangitis + tuberculous lymphadenitis of regional nodesApical cavitation
Lymph nodesInvolvedNot involved
Complications—Haemoptysis; pneumothorax (air in pleura); right-sided heart failure from lung fibrosis; amyloidosis (insoluble protein deposits)
Primary = "Ghon + 2 L's" (Lymphangitis, Lymphadenitis)Secondary = "Apex, Adult, Absent nodes".
Secondary TB complications: "Have Pity, Right Amy"Haemoptysis, Pneumothorax, Right heart failure, Amyloidosis.
Secondary TB has no lymph node involvement; primary TB has it. Right-sided (not left) heart failure follows lung fibrosis. The cavity is apical.

Tuberculosis · slides 23–31

Intestinal TB, tuberculous peritonitis and Pott's disease

Primary intestinal TBSecondary intestinal TB
LesionPrimary intestinal complex: tubercles at Peyer's patches, TB ulcer, tuberculous lymphangitis, tabes mesenterica (caseating mesenteric nodes)Tubercles in Peyer's patches of the terminal ileum, with tuberculous ulcers
Ulcers—Multiple, undermined edges, soft caseous floor, transverse, heal by fibrosis
LymphaticsInvolvedNo lymphangitis, no lymphadenitis

Tuberculous peritonitis TB 27

  • A secondary type, common in children.
  • Wet (ascitic) type: mainly exudative.
  • Dry (adhesive) type: mainly proliferative (cellular, tubercle-forming).

Pott's disease (spinal TB) TB 29–30

  • Cause: secondary, by the blood.
  • Sites: cervical, thoracic, lumbar.
  • Features: kyphosis (backward curvature), cold abscess, paraplegia.
  • Scoliosis = lateral curvature, for contrast.

Summary slide TB 31: a cold abscess is an accumulation of caseation in a localised area; caseation necrosis is characteristic of TB.

TB ulcer is a belt: it runs Transverse around the gutFollowing the lymphatics round the bowel; healing by fibrosis can then narrow it. The ulcer is "Multiple, Undermined, Soft-floored, Transverse".
Wet = Weeping (exudate), Dry = Dense (cells, adhesions)Tuberculous peritonitis types.
Pott's "KAP": Kyphosis, Abscess (cold), ParaplegiaSpread to the spine by the blood.
Tabes mesenterica belongs to the primary intestinal complex. Secondary intestinal TB has no lymphangitis. TB ulcers are transverse (typhoid ulcers are the longitudinal ones). A cold abscess is caseous material, not pus from acute infection.

Circulatory disorders · slides 2–9

Ischaemia and its clinical faces

Ischaemia CD 2: an inadequate blood supply to an organ or part. It causes hypoxia, failure to remove waste and malnutrition, leading to reversible cell injury, intracellular accumulations or necrosis.

ConditionWhat happens
Raynaud's disease CD 3–4A rare vessel disorder, usually fingers and toes. Vessels narrow with cold or stress → skin turns white and blue
Claudication CD 5Cramping leg pain induced by exercise, typically from arterial obstruction
Angina pectoris CD 6–7Chest pain from coronary ischaemia; a symptom of coronary artery disease; squeezing, pressure, heaviness, tightness
Varicose veins and ulcer CD 8–9Swollen, dilated, tortuous leg veins from incompetent valves; ischaemia of the overlying skin → varicose ulcer
Four faces of ischaemia: Fingers, Legs, Heart, SkinRaynaud's (fingers, cold), claudication (legs, walking), angina (heart, effort), varicose ulcer (skin over bad veins).
Ischaemia can cause reversible injury; infarction is the necrosis. Raynaud's is triggered by cold or stress, not exercise. Varicose veins come from incompetent valves.

Circulatory disorders · slides 10–17

Infarction and how the gut gets infarcted

Infarction CD 10: necrosis of tissue due to a cut in blood supply (complete, prolonged ischaemia).

TypeSitesWhy
Red (haemorrhagic)Lung, intestineLoose organs with a double blood supply and venous cut first; blood escapes from damaged capillaries into the infarct
PaleHeart, kidney, spleenSolid organs with an arterial cut first; starts red, then the blood is removed and it turns pale
SoftCentral nervous systemLiquefactive necrosis from lysosomal enzymes released by microglia or necrotic tissue

Pictures: infarction of kidney CD 11, myocardial infarction CD 12, lung CD 13, small intestine CD 14.

Intestinal causeMechanism
Strangulated hernia CD 15Vessels of the herniated loop are obstructed while passing through a narrow opening
Volvulus CD 16Twisting of an intestinal loop, obstructing vessels in its mesentery
Intussusception CD 17Invagination of one loop of intestine into another (intussusceptum inside the intussuscipiens)
Red = "Lungs and Loops" (loose, double supply). Pale = "HKS": Heart, Kidney, Spleen. Soft = brainVenous first → red. Arterial first → pale. Brain liquefies.
Gut killers: Squeezed, Twisted, TelescopedStrangulated hernia, volvulus, intussusception.
The lung gives a red infarct, not pale. The spleen gives a pale infarct. CNS infarcts are liquefactive, not coagulative. Pale infarcts start red.

Circulatory disorders · slides 18–26

Virchow's triad: the causes of thrombosis

Virchow's triad CD 18 lists the three causes of thromboembolism:

Arm of the triadCauses in the lecture
Hypercoagulability CD 19↑ blood viscosity (dehydration, malignant tumours); cancer treatment (radiation, chemotherapy); ↑ number and adhesiveness of platelets; ↓ heparin; genetic deficiencies or autoimmune disorders
Endothelial cell injury CD 20Atherosclerosis, surgery, pressure, trauma, inflammation of the artery
Disturbed blood flow (stasis) CD 21Leg veins after surgery, after childbirth or on a long flight; chronic venous congestion in heart failure and atrial fibrillation; acute inflammation; aneurysm (localised dilatation of an artery or the heart) and varicose veins

Picture slides CD 22–26: atherosclerosis, aneurysm, varicose vein, acute inflammation, increased platelets and viscosity, heart failure and AF, childbirth.

Virchow = "Thick, Torn, Slow"Thick blood (hypercoagulable), Torn wall (endothelial injury), Slow flow (stasis).
Stasis is "Sit, Surgery, Stork, Sick heart"Long flights, after surgery, after childbirth, heart failure and AF. Add the bulges: aneurysm and varicose veins.
Atherosclerosis is listed under endothelial injury; aneurysm and varicose veins under disturbed flow. Decreased (not increased) heparin causes hypercoagulability. Dehydration raises viscosity.

Circulatory disorders · slides 25–29

How a thrombus forms, and what happens to it

Slides 25–26 picture more causes from the triad: increased platelets, increased viscosity, heart failure and AF, and childbirth.

Pathogenesis of thrombosis CD 27–28

  1. After vascular injury, platelets are exposed to extracellular matrix (ECM): collagen, proteoglycan, fibronectin and adhesive glycoproteins.
  2. Platelet–ECM adhesion is mediated by von Willebrand factor (vWF), a bridge between platelet receptors and the matrix.
  3. Release reaction (granule secretion): alpha granules hold coagulation factors and growth factors; delta granules hold ADP, calcium and vasoactive amines.
  4. Aggregation, helped by a surface phospholipid complex that provides a site for calcium.
  5. Red cells and leukocytes join the haemostatic plug; leukocytes stick to platelets via P-selectin and add an inflammatory response.
  6. Lines of Zahn: alternating layers of platelets with fibrin, and red cells.
  7. The thrombus is attached to the vessel wall.

The diagram on slide 27 shows the same story in three stages: platelets attach to the injured endothelium, release fibrin and seal it, then a fibrin network traps red cells.

Fate of a thrombus CD 29

FateWhat happens
DissolutionRemoved by fibrinolytic activity
PropagationGathers more platelets and fibrin → obstructs the vessel
EmbolizationA piece breaks off: non-infected embolus → infarction; infected embolus → pyaemia
Organization and recanalizationInduces inflammation and fibrosis; may become recanalized (new channels)
CalcificationCalcified venous thrombus = phlebolith
Building a clot: "Stick, Bridge, Spill, Clump, Catch, Stripe, Stay"Stick to collagen, Bridge with vWF, Spill granules, Clump (aggregate), Catch red and white cells, Stripes of Zahn, Stay attached to the wall.
Alpha = Assembly kit, Delta = DenseAlpha granules carry the clotting and growth factors; delta (dense) granules carry ADP, calcium and amines.
Five fates: "Don't Panic, Everyone Orders Coffee"Dissolution, Propagation, Embolization, Organization, Calcification.
An infected embolus gives pyaemia; a non-infected one gives infarction. A phlebolith is a calcified thrombus. ADP and calcium are in delta, not alpha, granules.

Circulatory disorders · slides 30–34

Types of thrombosis: veins, arteries, heart

SiteTypeKey point
Veins CD 30–31PhlebothrombosisVenous thrombosis without inflammation
ThrombophlebitisVenous thrombosis due to inflammation
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)Thrombus in a deep vein, most often the leg (e.g. femoral vein)
Budd-Chiari syndromeBlockage of the hepatic vein or inferior vena cava → abdominal pain, ascites, hepatomegaly
Arteries CD 32–33StrokeRapid decline of brain function from ↓ blood supply; caused by ischaemia, thrombus, embolus or haemorrhage; a thrombotic stroke forms around atherosclerotic plaques
Myocardial infarctionComplete ischaemia, often a coronary artery thrombus → too little oxygen → heart muscle death
Heart CD 34VegetationsOn the valve surface in endocarditis
Mural thrombusOn the wall opposite a myocardial infarction
Ball thrombusInside a dilated left atrium in severe mitral stenosis
"Phlebo-thrombosis = plain clot · Thrombo-phleb-itis = -itis, inflamed"The one that ends in -itis is the inflamed one.
Heart clots: "Valves Vegetate, Murals Mirror MI, Balls fill a Big atrium"Endocarditis → vegetations; MI → mural thrombus opposite it; mitral stenosis → ball thrombus in the dilated left atrium.
Budd-Chiari = "Belly Big, Chiari Can't drain the liver"Hepatic vein or IVC blocked → pain, ascites, big liver.
Phlebothrombosis has no inflammation; thrombophlebitis is caused by it. Budd-Chiari is the hepatic vein or IVC, not the portal vein. A mural thrombus sits opposite an MI; a ball thrombus is in the left atrium.

Memory aids

Hooks, numbers and traps

Read these out loud, then test yourself in the Flashcards. The key-facts grid is your last-hour sheet.

How questions catch you

Trick 1Primary vs secondary

Lymph nodes, Ghon's focus, apical cavity, tabes mesenterica: which form has which.

Trick 2Red vs pale

Lung and intestine are red; heart, kidney and spleen are pale; brain is soft.

Trick 3Wrong arm of the triad

Atherosclerosis = endothelial injury; aneurysm = disturbed flow; dehydration = hypercoagulability.

Trick 4Immunity vs hypersensitivity

One makes the tubercle, the other makes caseation.

Trick 5Direction words

Transverse ulcer, apical cavity, kyphosis backward, scoliosis lateral, right-sided failure.

Trick 6Spread route

Inhalation or milk to start; blood for miliary TB and Pott's disease.
